files.README.md:
# Freelance First Portfolio Kit

Build a small, honest, convincing portfolio when you don't have client work yet, in about four weeks of part-time effort.

## What's inside

| File | What it's for |
|---|---|
| 01-positioning-worksheet.md | Decide who the portfolio is for and write your one-sentence positioning |
| 02-project-briefs.md | Ten realistic project briefs across common freelance services, plus a blank brief |
| 03-case-study-template.md | Fill-in template for writing each project up |
| 04-worked-example.md | A complete example: brief, work log and finished case study |
| 05-portfolio-page-outline.md | Section-by-section outline and wording for your portfolio page |
| 06-launch-checklist.md | Checks before you share the link, and how to start using it |
| four-week-plan.csv | Day-by-day plan you can tick off |
| project-log.csv | Time and decision log to keep while you work |

## How to use it

1. **Day 1:** Fill in the positioning worksheet. Don't skip this; every other step depends on it.
2. **Days 2-3:** Pick three briefs from `02-project-briefs.md` (or write your own with the blank brief). Aim for one redesign/rewrite, one invented brief done end to end, and one real-world or volunteer piece.
3. **Weeks 1-3:** Do one project at a time. Log time and decisions in `project-log.csv` as you go.
4. **Week 4:** Write each case study with `03-case-study-template.md`, build your page with `05-portfolio-page-outline.md`, run the launch checklist and send it to your first prospects.

## Ground rules

- **Label concept work honestly.** Every self-initiated project should say so. Buyers respect it; they don't forgive being misled.
- **No real brands as fake clients.** If you redesign something that exists, describe the business generically and don't use its logo or name as if they hired you.
- **No invented results or testimonials.** For concept work, say what you *would* measure. Only quote real people, with permission.
- **Three good pieces, then ship.** Polishing a fourth piece is usually a way of avoiding outreach.

Replace each concept piece with real client work as soon as you have it, weakest first.

# Positioning Worksheet

Your portfolio needs a target. Work through these questions in one sitting (about 45 minutes), then write your positioning sentence at the end.

## Part 1: What you can deliver

List the deliverables you can produce to a professional standard today. Be concrete: "a five-page small business website", not "web stuff".

| Deliverable | How confident am I? (1-5) | Do I enjoy it? (1-5) |
|---|---|---|
| | | |
| | | |
| | | |
| | | |

Circle the one or two that score highest on both.

## Part 2: Who you understand

List types of business or organisation you know from the inside: a past job, a family business, a hobby, a community you're part of.

| Type of business | How I know it | One problem I've seen them struggle with |
|---|---|---|
| | | |
| | | |
| | | |

Insider knowledge is your shortcut. Your concept projects will be far more believable for a business type you understand.

## Part 3: Can they pay?

For each business type you listed, answer:

- Do they already spend money on this kind of work? (yes / sometimes / rarely)
- Can you name at least 20 of them you could reach? (yes / no)
- Is the deliverable tied to money for them (bookings, sales, enquiries, saved time)? (yes / no)

Cross out any business type with two or more "no / rarely" answers.

## Part 4: Write your positioning sentence

> I help **[type of business]** with **[specific deliverable]** so they can **[outcome they care about]**.

Examples:

- I help independent cafes with menus and social graphics so they can sell more of their high-margin items.
- I help small accounting firms rewrite their websites so they get more enquiries from the clients they actually want.
- I help online course creators set up email sequences so new subscribers become paying students.

My sentence:

> I help ______________________ with ______________________ so they can ______________________.

## Part 5: Sanity check

- [ ] Could a stranger tell from this sentence whether they're the right kind of client?
- [ ] Could I make three portfolio projects that fit it?
- [ ] Would I be happy doing this kind of work for six months?

If you can tick all three, move on. You can refine it after your first few client conversations.
files.02-project-briefs.md:
# Project Briefs

Ten realistic briefs for self-initiated portfolio projects. Each has a business, a problem, a goal, constraints and deliverables, like a real client job. Pick the ones that match your positioning, adjust the details to the business type you chose, and respect the time limit.

All businesses below are invented. If you base a project on a real business you've seen, describe it generically ("a family-run hardware shop") and don't present it as a client.

---

## 1. Homepage rewrite: small physiotherapy clinic (copywriting)

- **Business:** Two-practitioner clinic in a mid-sized town. Most clients are 35-65 with back, knee or sports injuries.
- **Problem:** The homepage lists treatments and qualifications but never says who they help or how to book. Most visitors leave without acting.
- **Goal:** Make booking an appointment the obvious next step for a first-time visitor.
- **Constraints:** 8 hours. Existing site layout stays; you're changing words only. Must avoid medical claims.
- **Deliverables:** Rewritten homepage copy (headline, intro, three service blocks, FAQ of five questions, call to action), plus a one-paragraph rationale.

## 2. Menu redesign: neighbourhood cafe (graphic design)

- **Business:** Independent cafe, 30 seats, breakfast and lunch. Strong coffee, under-ordered food.
- **Problem:** The A3 menu is crowded, uses four fonts, and the most profitable items are buried.
- **Goal:** A menu that's easy to scan and nudges people toward the three highest-margin dishes.
- **Constraints:** 10 hours. Must print on a standard home or office printer. Existing brand colour is dark green.
- **Deliverables:** Print-ready menu (front and back), a small table tent version, before-and-after comparison.

## 3. Five-page website: independent dog groomer (web design/development)

- **Business:** One-person grooming studio, appointment only.
- **Problem:** Currently only has a social media page; customers keep messaging to ask prices and availability.
- **Goal:** A simple site that answers the common questions and sends people to book.
- **Constraints:** 15 hours. Must work well on phones. Owner needs to update prices herself.
- **Deliverables:** Home, Services and Prices, About, FAQ, Contact/Book pages, and a one-page handover note for the owner.

## 4. Welcome email sequence: online pottery course (email marketing)

- **Business:** Solo creator selling a self-paced beginner pottery course.
- **Problem:** 2,000 newsletter subscribers, very few buy. New subscribers get one generic welcome email.
- **Goal:** A sequence that builds trust and makes a clear, low-pressure offer.
- **Constraints:** 8 hours. Five emails maximum. Plain text style, no heavy design.
- **Deliverables:** Five emails with subject lines, send timing, and one paragraph on the strategy.

## 5. Bookkeeping clean-up process: small landscaping company (bookkeeping/admin)

- **Business:** Owner-run landscaping company with two seasonal staff.
- **Problem:** Receipts in a shoebox, invoices sent late, owner spends Sunday nights on paperwork.
- **Goal:** A simple monthly routine that takes under two hours.
- **Constraints:** 8 hours. Assume a basic spreadsheet only, no paid software.
- **Deliverables:** Monthly checklist, a receipt and invoice tracking spreadsheet with sample data, and a one-page guide for the owner.

## 6. Social content plan: local bike repair shop (social media)

- **Business:** Repair-focused bike shop that also sells a few accessories.
- **Problem:** Posts are irregular and mostly photos of stock. Followers don't engage.
- **Goal:** A month of content that shows expertise and brings people in for services.
- **Constraints:** 10 hours. Owner can spend 20 minutes a day posting; content must be shootable on a phone.
- **Deliverables:** 4-week content calendar, 12 written captions, 3 example post designs or mock-ups, a short shot list.

## 7. Product photography set: handmade candle brand (photography)

- **Business:** Small-batch candle maker selling online.
- **Problem:** Product photos are inconsistent and shot on a kitchen counter.
- **Goal:** A consistent set of product images that look good together on a shop page.
- **Constraints:** One day of shooting, natural light or a single lamp, props under a small budget.
- **Deliverables:** 10 edited photos (white background and lifestyle), a one-page style guide so the owner can reshoot new products to match.

## 8. Onboarding guide: software for dental receptionists (technical writing)

- **Business:** Invented scheduling tool for small dental practices.
- **Problem:** New receptionists keep calling support with the same ten questions.
- **Goal:** A guide that gets a new user confident in their first hour.
- **Constraints:** 10 hours. Plain language, assume no technical background.
- **Deliverables:** A 6-8 page getting-started guide, a one-page quick reference, and a list of the questions it answers.

## 9. Brand refresh: family-run plumbing business (branding)

- **Business:** Second-generation plumbing company, three vans, mostly residential.
- **Problem:** Logo is from the 1990s, vans and invoices all look different.
- **Goal:** A modest refresh that looks trustworthy and is easy to apply consistently.
- **Constraints:** 15 hours. Must keep the family name prominent. Must work in one colour on van livery.
- **Deliverables:** Updated logo (full and compact), colour and type choices, a two-page mini style guide, mock-ups on a van, invoice and business card.

## 10. Data dashboard: membership-based climbing gym (data/analysis)

- **Business:** Climbing gym with about 600 members.
- **Problem:** The manager exports membership data monthly but never knows if things are getting better or worse.
- **Goal:** A simple monthly view of joins, cancellations and visit patterns.
- **Constraints:** 12 hours. Use invented sample data. Must be understandable by a non-technical manager.
- **Deliverables:** A spreadsheet or dashboard with five key charts, the sample dataset, and a one-page "how to read this" note.

---

## Blank brief

- **Business:** (what they sell, to whom, roughly how big)
- **Problem:** (one specific thing that isn't working)
- **Goal:** (what would be different if this worked)
- **Constraints:** (time limit, budget level, things that can't change)
- **Deliverables:** (exactly what you'll hand over)
- **How success would be measured:** (what a real client would watch)

# Case Study Template

Use one copy per project. Target 250-400 words. Fill in the brackets, then delete the guidance lines.

---

## [Project title: what you did, for what kind of business]

*Example: "Making booking obvious: homepage rewrite for a small physiotherapy clinic"*

**Project type:** [Self-initiated concept project / Volunteer project for ___ / Personal product]
**Deliverable:** [What you produced]
**Time:** [Hours spent, from your project log]

### In one line

[One sentence a busy client could read and understand. What you did and why it matters.]

### The situation

[2-3 sentences. Who is the business, who are their customers, and what specifically wasn't working? Be concrete: "The homepage never mentions how to book" beats "The site felt dated".]

### What I did

[3-5 short points or a short paragraph. Cover the main steps and, most importantly, one or two decisions you made and why. Decisions show judgement, and judgement is what clients pay for.]

- [Step or decision]
- [Step or decision]
- [Step or decision]

### Before and after

[Images, excerpts or a short side-by-side. Point out the one or two changes that matter most.]

### How success would be measured

[For concept work you can't claim results. Instead, say what a real client should watch and roughly what "better" looks like. Example: "The share of homepage visitors who click 'Book an appointment', checked monthly."]

### What I'd do next

[Optional, 1-2 sentences. What you'd test or add with more time or a real client. Shows you think beyond the deliverable.]

---

## Before you publish

- [ ] The project type label is visible near the top
- [ ] No real brand logo or name is used as if they were a client
- [ ] No invented results, numbers or testimonials
- [ ] At least one decision is explained, not just described
- [ ] A client could understand it without seeing the images
- [ ] Under 400 words
files.04-worked-example.md:
# Worked Example

A complete run-through of one project, from brief to finished case study. The freelancer, Sam, is a new copywriter whose positioning is: *"I help small health and wellness clinics rewrite their websites so more visitors book an appointment."*

## 1. The brief (from 02-project-briefs.md, adjusted)

- **Business:** Two-practitioner physiotherapy clinic in a mid-sized town. Clients mostly 35-65 with back, knee or sports injuries.
- **Problem:** Homepage lists treatments and qualifications, never says who they help or how to book.
- **Goal:** Make booking the obvious next step for a first-time visitor.
- **Constraints:** 8 hours. Words only, layout stays. No medical claims.
- **Deliverables:** Rewritten homepage copy, five-question FAQ, one-paragraph rationale.
- **How success would be measured:** Share of homepage visitors clicking "Book an appointment".

## 2. Sam's project log (excerpt)

| Date | Hours | Task | Decision / note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mon | 1.5 | Read 8 clinic homepages in similar towns, noted patterns | Most lead with credentials. Almost none say who they're for. Opportunity. |
| Mon | 1.0 | Listed 15 questions a first-time patient would have | Top 3: "Can you help with my problem?", "Do I need a referral?", "How soon can I be seen?" |
| Tue | 2.0 | First draft of headline, intro and service blocks | Dropped treatment jargon. Grouped services by problem (back, knee, sport) not by technique. |
| Tue | 0.5 | Read it aloud | Intro too long. Cut from 90 to 45 words. |
| Wed | 1.5 | FAQ and calls to action | Put "Book an appointment" after intro and after each service block, not only at the bottom. |
| Wed | 1.0 | Rationale and final edit | Removed one sentence that read like a promise of recovery. Kept to general information. |
| **Total** | **7.5** | | |

## 3. The finished case study

### Making booking obvious: homepage rewrite for a small physiotherapy clinic

**Project type:** Self-initiated concept project
**Deliverable:** Homepage copy and FAQ
**Time:** 7.5 hours

#### In one line

I rewrote a clinic homepage around the questions first-time patients actually ask, so that booking becomes the natural next step instead of something they have to hunt for.

#### The situation

Many small physiotherapy clinics open their homepage with a list of techniques and qualifications. That reassures other professionals, but a person with a sore back mostly wants to know: can you help me, and how do I book? This concept clinic's page answered neither.

#### What I did

- Reviewed eight similar clinic homepages and listed the fifteen questions a first-time patient is likely to have.
- Reorganised services by problem (back and neck, knees and hips, sports injuries) instead of by technique, because patients search by what hurts, not by treatment name.
- Cut the introduction from 90 to 45 words and led with who the clinic helps.
- Added a booking button after the intro and after each service block, so it's always one tap away on a phone.
- Wrote a five-question FAQ covering referrals, waiting times, what to wear, first appointment length and cancellation.

#### Before and after

Before: *"Our chartered physiotherapists offer manual therapy, dry needling, and exercise rehabilitation..."*
After: *"Back, knee or sports injury slowing you down? We're a small local clinic that sees most new patients within the week. Book your first appointment online in two minutes."*

#### How success would be measured

The share of homepage visitors who click "Book an appointment", compared month on month, plus the number of phone calls asking basic questions the FAQ now answers.

#### What I'd do next

Test two headline versions with a real clinic, and add a short "what happens at your first visit" section.

---

## Why this works

- The label is honest and right at the top.
- It explains decisions (grouping by problem, booking button placement), not just output.
- It doesn't claim results it can't have. It says what to measure.
- A clinic owner reading it would recognise their own homepage problem.

# Portfolio Page Outline

One page is enough to start. It should load fast, work on a phone, and make the first screen do the selling. Fill in each section below.

## 1. Top of page (the first screen)

- **Headline:** your positioning sentence, or a shorter version of it.
  - *Example:* "Website copy for small health clinics that turns visitors into bookings."
- **One supporting line:** who you are and what happens next.
  - *Example:* "I'm Sam, a copywriter working with independent clinics. Send me your homepage and I'll reply with three quick fixes."
- **Contact button:** "Email me" or "Get in touch". Link it directly.

## 2. Work (three project cards)

For each project:

- Image or short excerpt
- Project title
- The "In one line" sentence from your case study
- Project type label (self-initiated, volunteer, personal)
- Link to the full case study

Put your strongest, most relevant project first.

**Honesty line under the cards (suggested wording):**

> These are self-initiated and volunteer projects, built to the same briefs and time limits I use for client work. I'm currently taking on my first paid projects in this area.

## 3. How I work

Three or four short steps a client can picture. Example:

1. **Short call (20 minutes):** you tell me what's not working.
2. **Proposal within 2 working days:** scope, price and timeline in writing.
3. **First draft within a week,** then up to two rounds of changes.
4. **Handover:** final files plus a short note on how to use them.

## 4. About

Three to five sentences focused on clients, not your life story. Include one piece of relevant background (past job, industry knowledge, training) that makes you more believable for this kind of business.

## 5. Contact (repeat)

- The same contact button as the top
- What happens after they get in touch ("I reply within one working day")
- Optional: rough starting price or "projects typically start from..." to filter out poor fits

## Page checklist

- [ ] First screen says what you do and for whom, without scrolling
- [ ] Contact link at top and bottom
- [ ] Exactly three projects, most relevant first
- [ ] Every project labelled with its type
- [ ] Loads and reads well on a phone
- [ ] No typos (read it aloud once)
files.06-launch-checklist.md:
# Launch Checklist

Run through this before you send your portfolio link to anyone, then use the outreach section to start getting real work.

## Before sharing

- [ ] Positioning sentence is on the first screen
- [ ] Three projects, each with a written case study
- [ ] Each project clearly labelled (self-initiated, volunteer or personal)
- [ ] No real company presented as a client; no borrowed logos
- [ ] No invented numbers, results or testimonials
- [ ] Contact link works (send yourself a test message)
- [ ] Opened and checked on a phone
- [ ] Asked one person outside your field to look at it for 30 seconds and tell you what you do. If they can't, fix the top of the page.

## Week one of outreach

- [ ] List 20 businesses that match your positioning sentence
- [ ] For each, note one specific thing you noticed (a problem your projects show you can fix)
- [ ] Send 10 short, personal messages linking to the single most relevant project, not the whole portfolio
- [ ] Follow up once, 4-5 working days later, with one extra useful idea
- [ ] Log every message and reply

## Getting your first real proof

- [ ] If you did a volunteer project, ask for a short testimonial in their own words, and permission to use their name
- [ ] After your first paid project, write it up with the same template within a week, while details are fresh
- [ ] Replace your weakest concept piece with the real project
- [ ] Update the honesty line once most work on the page is paid client work

## Monthly review (15 minutes)

- [ ] Which project gets the most clicks or mentions in replies? Move it first.
- [ ] Is your positioning still right, based on who actually replies?
- [ ] Any concept piece you can now replace?
